rows.sentence: Based on the article in the document, the medication your friend is referring to is **tirzepatide**, sold under the brand names Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes) and Zepbound (for obesity).
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article identifies tirzepatide and gives both brand names and their respective indications.

rows.sentence: The article reports on two new studies, the SURMOUNT-OSA trials, showing that tirzepatide "significantly reduces sleep disruptions" in patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The title and opening describe the reduction in sleep disruptions, and the article identifies the two studies as SURMOUNT-OSA.

rows.sentence: Tirzepatide is described as a long-acting glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article explicitly gives this description of the drug.

rows.sentence: In the studies, participants received the maximum tolerated dose (10 or 15 mg) by once-weekly injection for one year.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article confirms this dose, schedule, and duration for participants assigned to tirzepatide.

rows.sentence: The connection runs through obesity.
rows.label: unsupported
rows.rationale: The article identifies obesity as a risk factor but does not establish that tirzepatide improves OSA through weight loss rather than through an independent effect.

rows.sentence: The article notes that OSA affects 1 billion people worldwide and 30 million American adults, many undiagnosed, and that obesity is a common risk factor: 40% of people with obesity have OSA, and 70% of people with OSA have obesity.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article explicitly states both prevalence figures, notes that many people are undiagnosed, and gives the two percentages linking OSA and obesity.

rows.sentence: The trials enrolled patients with obesity (BMI of 30 kg/m² or greater) and moderate-to-severe OSA (more than 15 events per hour on the apnea–hypopnea index, or AHI).
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article gives the same BMI and AHI thresholds for enrollment.

rows.sentence: At baseline, 65% to 70% of participants had severe OSA, with more than 30 events per hour and a mean of 51.5.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article reports the same baseline percentage, severity threshold, and mean.

rows.sentence: Because clinical guidelines already recommend weight-loss strategies as part of OSA treatment — even though, as one editorial noted, "the integration of obesity management into the approaches to care for obstructive sleep apnea has lagged" — an effective obesity medication is an "obvious avenue to pursue."
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The editorial describes the guideline recommendation and the lag in practice, and explicitly presents an effective obesity medication as an avenue to pursue.

rows.sentence: In the two double-blind randomized controlled trials (conducted at 60 sites in nine countries, presented at the ADA 84th Scientific Sessions and published in the New England Journal of Medicine), by one year patients taking tirzepatide had 27 to 30 fewer AHI events per hour, compared with only 4 to 6 fewer for placebo.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article confirms the trial design and locations, where the results were presented and published, and both one-year reductions.

rows.sentence: Up to half of those receiving tirzepatide in both trials reached an AHI of less than 5 or 5 to 14 events per hour and an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 10 or less — thresholds the authors say "represent a level at which CPAP therapy may not be recommended."
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article reports the same proportion and thresholds and quotes the authors' interpretation of those thresholds for CPAP.

rows.sentence: Consequently, 40% to 50% of patients no longer needed to use a CPAP device.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article's opening explicitly links the reduction in sleep disruptions to this reported percentage no longer needing CPAP.

rows.sentence: Patients lost 18% to 20% of their body weight.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article reports this range of weight loss for patients taking tirzepatide.

rows.sentence: Tirzepatide also lowered C-reactive protein levels and systolic blood pressure (by 9.7 mm Hg in study 1 and 7.6 mm Hg in study 2 at Week 48).
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article reports both reductions and gives the same week-48 blood-pressure figures for the two studies.

rows.sentence: The accompanying editorial noted this blood-pressure improvement "was substantially larger than effects seen with CPAP therapy alone," suggesting tirzepatide "may be an attractive option for those patients who seek to reduce their cardiovascular risk."
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article attributes both the comparison with CPAP alone and the suggestion about cardiovascular risk to the editorial.

rows.sentence: Patients also reported fewer daytime and nighttime disturbances, measured using the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form scale for Sleep-Related Impairment and Sleep Disturbance.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article reports fewer disturbances and names the same measurement instrument.

rows.sentence: CPAP is the most-used and effective intervention for OSA, but many patients refuse it, stop using it, or cannot use it, and as many as half abandon CPAP within 3 years.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article describes CPAP as effective and most used, and it gives both the barriers to use and the three-year abandonment estimate.

rows.sentence: If tirzepatide eventually gains FDA approval for OSA, it would be the first drug approved for the condition, offering "a more accessible alternative" for people who cannot tolerate or adhere to existing therapies.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article states that approval would make tirzepatide the first approved drug for OSA and quotes Malhotra describing it as a more accessible alternative for those patients.

rows.sentence: However, the article includes cautions.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article explicitly raises a concern about whether patients would stay on treatment outside a trial.

rows.sentence: The most common adverse events were diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting, occurring in about a quarter of patients, and there were two adjudicated-confirmed cases of acute pancreatitis in study 2.
rows.label: supported
rows.rationale: The article lists the same adverse events and frequency for tirzepatide recipients and reports two confirmed pancreatitis cases in study 2.

rows.sentence: The editorial also raised concerns about whether patients outside a trial would stick with therapy (citing high discontinuation rates for GLP-1 receptor agonists) and about racial disparities in access to these drugs.
rows.label: unsupported
rows.rationale: The adherence concern is explicit, but the editorial identifies racial disparities in drug use among patients with diabetes and warns about disparities in OSA care; it does not explicitly identify disparities in access to the drugs.

rows.sentence: Finally, experts noted it is still unclear whether tirzepatide had an independent effect on OSA or whether the results were primarily due to weight loss; one expert said, "I believe that over time we'll see that this particular effect in sleep apnea is related to weight."
rows.label: unsupported
rows.rationale: The article attributes both the uncertainty and the quoted prediction to Louis Aronne alone; it does not report that multiple experts noted this uncertainty.

rows.sentence: Another expert commented that "the treatment of obesity with tirzepatide plus CPAP is really the optimal treatment for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity-related cardiometabolic risks."
rows.label: contradictory
rows.rationale: The article attributes this comment to Louis Aronne, the same expert quoted in the previous sentence, not to a different expert.

rows.sentence: In short, the article presents tirzepatide as a promising option that attacks the obesity underlying OSA, with large reductions in apnea events, daytime sleepiness, and cardiovascular risk markers — and the possible elimination of CPAP for some patients — while noting it is not yet FDA-approved for OSA and carries side effects and long-term adherence questions.
rows.label: unsupported
rows.rationale: The article reports weight loss but leaves its role in the OSA improvement unresolved. It also reports fewer disturbances and an Epworth score threshold, not a large measured reduction in daytime sleepiness.
